background.definition: Encephalitis is an inflammatory process of the brain accompanied by clinical evidence of neurologic dysfunction; viruses are the most common pathogens.

list.listitem: Herpes encephalitis affects 1 in 500,000 persons annually.
Arboviral encephalitis affects approximately 150 to 3000 cases per year.
Most common worldwide is Japanese encephalitis with about 50,000 cases per year.
More than 50 identified pathogens may cause encephalitis. Most common etiologies in the United States are herpes simplex virus (HSV), West Nile virus, and the enteroviruses.
Despite extensive diagnostics, in many cases (up to 75% in some studies), the etiology remains unknown.
The incidence of encephalitis caused by vaccine preventable conditions such as measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella is decreasing.
Less commonly caused by bacteria (ie, Bartonella species, L. monocytogenes, M. pneumoniae, M. tuberculosis), rickettsioses, and fungi.
See for causes of viral encephalitis by region.
Primary encephalitis: direct invasion of virus into brain or spinal cord.
Secondary encephalitis: complication of viral infection or reactivation of latent virus.
Once across the blood-brain barrier, viruses can enter cells and disrupt cell functioning, cause perivascular congestion, and damage by inflammatory response.
Primary prevention: protective clothing and DEET containing repellants will prevent mosquito-borne transmission. A
Universal immunization is recommended for measles, mumps, rubella, and poliovirus. A
Suspect encephalitis in patients with acute onset of fever, mental status changes, and headache. C
Ask about risk factors and epidemiologic clues to the etiology (ie, travel, insect bites). C
CSF analysis is essential for diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Delirium secondary to toxins, drugs, psychosis

Differential.Differential_Features: Known antigenic stimulus (vaccine or viral syndrome), lack of fever at onset, younger age of onset
Aura, lack of fever or altered mentation

list.listitem: Presentation may be acute or subacute depending on the etiology of encephalitis. Patients may have prodromal illness and typically present with altered sensorium, fever and may have focal neurological deficits and seizures. See for symptoms as they relate to specific types of encephalitis.
Epidemiologic clues: season, locale, local disease prevalence.
History: travel history, insect/animal contacts, occupational exposures, vaccination history, immune status, recreational activities.
summarizes the viral and bacterial pathogens associated with different animals.
Symptoms: viral prodrome, behavioral/personality changes, seizures, decreased level of consciousness.
Physical findings: altered mental status, focal hemiparesis, cranial nerve deficits, movement disorders.
Eighty percent of patients with herpes simplex encephalitis will have focal neurologic deficits.
CSF analysis: typically will see 5 to 500 white blood cells (mostly lymphocytes), normal glucose, protein elevation >50 g/dL, significant numbers of RBCs; up to 10% will have normal findings.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of CSF: accurate for the detection of herpes viruses and enteroviruses, also can detect varicella zoster, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). VZV, CMV, EBV, and West Nile. PCR for HSV-1 and HSV-2 is 95% sensitive and 99% specific.
Culture of CSF: limited usefulness.
Neuroimaging: MRI is more sensitive than CT, and may show a high signal intensity lesion on T2-weighted and FLAIR images.
Brain biopsy is not routinely used, but should be considered when the etiology is unknown and the patient's condition is deteriorating despite treatment.
Without the identification of an etiologic agent, the diagnosis is presumptive and based on the clinical presentation.
Suspect encephalitis in patients with acute onset of fever, mental status changes, and headache.
Any patient with suspected encephalitis should undergo lumbar puncture and possible hospitalization for antiviral therapy.

Initial evaluation should also include lumbar puncture with specific pathogen testing (ELISA or PCR) individualized for epidemiological risk factors. Neuroimaging should also be considered for most patients (preferably MRI); viral culture is generally not helpful.
Empiric therapy should be initiated using acyclovir.
All cases of suspected encephalitis should be treated with acyclovir while an etiology is being sought. B
If another specifically treatable organism is not found or suspected (rickettsial or ehrlichial infection), all other treatment is supportive. C

Pending results of diagnostic studies, acyclovir therapy should be initiated. Recommendations below are from the Infectious Diseases Society of America guidelines although they have not been updated since 2008.
For HSV encephalitis, prescribe acyclovir 10mg/kg IV every 8 hours. Other antivirals include foscarnet and ganciclovir.
Other antimicrobial agents can be added if epidemiologic or clinical factors suggest a specific bacterial etiology.
EBV: acyclovir is not recommended, corticosteroids may be beneficial.
HIV encephalitis: highly active antiretroviral therapy is recommended.
Rickettsial disease: doxycycline is recommended.
Fungal infection: encephalitis due to fungal disease should be treated with an appropriate azole or amphotericin.
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (postinfectious or postvaccination): treat with high-dose corticosteroids; plasma exchange and IV immunoglobulin may also be considered.
Autoimmune encephalitis: systemic corticosteroids, IV immunoglobulin and plasma exchange
Selected patients may need neurosurgical evaluation if there is evidence of increased intracranial pressure.
Provide supportive therapy for all patients ( ie, hydration, monitoring, antipyretics, analgesics).
Treatment duration of acyclovir for herpes encephalitis is 14 to 21 days.
Complications associated with acute infection may include respiratory arrest, coma, seizures, increased intracranial pressure, syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH), and death.
Postinfection patients may have persistent neurologic dysfunction.
Full recovery may take months and neurologic complications may persist. B
In a series of 35 patients with herpes simplex encephalitis, mortality was 9%. Increasing age and lower albumin on admission predicted a worse outcome.
In a study of 40 children with herpes encephalitis, 14 had a poor outcome but there were no deaths.
In a series of 156 patients with encephalitis or meningoencephalitis caused by West Nile Virus, most recovered within 1 year. Recovery was faster in patients with fewer comorbidities. B

In a retrospective analysis of 103 patients in the ICU with encephalitis, death was associated with the presence of cerebral edema, status epilepticus and thrombocytopenia, as was respiratory failure requiring ventilator support.

feature.caption: Causes of Viral Encephalitis by Region and Vector.
feature.feature_body:
Viral Disease Location Vector/Host
Herpes simplex encephalitis Worldwide Human to human contact
West Nile encephalitis US, Africa, Middle East Mosquito (Aedes sp)/Birds
Western Equine encephalitis Western US and Canada Mosquito (Aedes and Culex sp)/birds
Eastern Equine encephalitis US: East Coast, Gulf Coast Mosquito (Aedes, Culex, Coquillettidia sp)/birds
Japanese encephalitis Asia Mosquito (Aedes sp)/birds, pigs
St. Louis encephalitis Midwestern US Mosquito(Culex sp)/birds
La Crosse encephalitis Throughout US
Aedes triseriatus/rodents
US denotes United States.
